links.why: Box states and the Pauli principle: the Fermi sea is $N$ particles in a box; the QM tunnelling room's $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V-E)}/\hbar$ uses the same $\hbar^2/2m$ scale.
Hydrostatic equilibrium and the virial theorem: here the pressure is Pauli pressure instead of gas or radiation pressure. Eddington's $L_{\rm Edd}$ and $M_{\rm Ch}$ both come from simple constants.
The CMB photon gas ($u=aT^4$) next to the phonon gas ($u\propto T^4/v^3$) of a crystal.
The astro Degenerate Vault: lessons and fights on white dwarfs, neutron stars and accretion (Choudhuri Ch. 5).

intro: One equation, three courses. Fill a box with fermions and you get a Fermi sea; in copper it sets the heat capacity and bulk modulus, in a white dwarf it holds up a star against gravity, and when the electrons turn relativistic it fixes the Chandrasekhar mass. The final boss of the Crystal Caverns ties QM, solid state and astro together.

blocks.html: QM: a particle in a box has $E\propto n^2/L^2$. Put $N$ fermions in: they stack up to the Fermi energy because each state holds two. Solid state: the conduction electrons of copper are exactly this with $n=8.5\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, $\epsilon_F=7$ eV. Astro: a white dwarf core is the same with $n\sim3\times10^{35}$ m$^{-3}$, $\epsilon_F\sim160$ keV.

blocks.label: Same formula in metals and white dwarfs (Choudhuri 5.9, 5.11).
Energy-balance estimate of the mass–radius relation and the limiting mass.

blocks.html: Why electrons and not nuclei? At equal number density electrons and nuclei have the same $p_F$, but pressure is a momentum flux $\sim p_Fv_F=p_F^2/m$, so the light electrons dominate by $m_p/m_e\approx2000$. Nuclei supply the mass (hence $\mu_e$), electrons the pressure.

Bosons with $\omega=vq$: photons ($v=c$, 2 polarisations) give $u=aT^4$ (CMB, stellar interiors); phonons ($v\sim3$ km/s, 3 polarisations) give Debye's $C\propto T^3$. Same integral, the speed enters as $1/v^3$.
Do not use the non-relativistic $\epsilon_F$ when $p_F\gtrsim m_ec$ (white dwarfs above $\sim10^9$ kg/m$^3$). In a metal $\epsilon_F\ll m_ec^2$ always.

Astro (Refregier/Choudhuri): degeneracy pressure, $R\propto M^{-1/3}$, $M_{\rm Ch}$. Solid state (HS23, HS20): $\epsilon_F$, $\nu(\epsilon_F)$, $c_V$ ratios. QM: box states, counting, Pauli. The Degenerate Core boss asks all three in one problem.

encounters.goal: For a gas of bosons with dispersion $\omega=vq$, $g$ polarisations and no cutoff, show $u=g\frac{\pi^2(k_BT)^4}{30(\hbar v)^3}$. Recover the Stefan–Boltzmann constant ($g=2$, $v=c$) and Debye's low-$T$ law ($g=3$).

encounters.title: From copper to a white dwarf: how degenerate is it?
encounters.problem: Cross-course (Solid State script 3.1, Astro Choudhuri §5.2). Electrons in a white dwarf core: density $\rho=10^{9}$ kg/m$^3$ (the typical value quoted by Choudhuri), carbon/oxygen so $\mu_e=2$ (one electron per two nucleons), $n_e=\rho/(\mu_em_H)$. The core temperature is $10^7$ K. Use exactly the same free-electron formulas as for copper.

steps.hint: Choudhuri eq. 5.6 with $\mu_e=2/(1+X)=2$ for $X=0$ (helium and heavier: half as many electrons as nucleons).
Same formula as copper (7 eV) with $n$ larger by $3.5\times10^6$: $\epsilon_F$ larger by $(3.5\times10^6)^{2/3}=2.3\times10^4$, i.e. $\approx160$ keV.
$k_BT=0.86$ keV for $10^7$ K, so $\epsilon_F/k_BT\approx190\gg1$: the electron gas is deeply degenerate, the protons/ions ($\epsilon_F\propto1/m$) are not (Choudhuri §5.2).

$x\approx0.8$: neither $\ll1$ nor $\gg1$, so at $10^9$ kg/m$^3$ the electrons are mildly relativistic (Choudhuri Fig. 5.1: relativistic effects start near $10^9$ kg/m$^3$). The two limits (5.9) and (5.11) bracket the real equation of state.

encounters.title: Degeneracy pressure: a coin of copper and a star
encounters.problem: The pressure of a degenerate non-relativistic Fermi gas is $P=\frac25n\epsilon_F$; the bulk modulus is $B=-V\,dP/dV=\frac53P$. In terms of density, Choudhuri (5.9)-(5.10): $P=K_1\rho^{5/3}$ with $K_1=\dfrac{3^{2/3}}{20\pi^{2/3}}\dfrac{h^2}{m_e\,m_H^{5/3}\mu_e^{5/3}}$. (a) Copper, $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$. (b) White dwarf core, $\rho=10^9$ kg/m$^3$, $\mu_e=2$.

steps.hint: Free-electron value $7.03$ eV.

steps.prompt: Degeneracy pressure of copper's electrons $P=\frac25n\epsilon_F$ in GPa.
steps.hint: $\approx38$ GPa $=3.8\times10^5$ atm. This is the repulsive pressure balanced by the ionic attraction (cohesion).

steps.prompt: Bulk modulus of the free-electron gas $B=\frac53P=\frac23n\epsilon_F$ in GPa.
steps.hint: $64$ GPa versus the measured $140$ GPa: the right order of magnitude from Pauli exclusion alone. A classical gas would give $B=nk_BT\sim10^{-4}$ GPa.

steps.prompt: The Choudhuri constant $K_1$ in SI units ($P=K_1\rho^{5/3}$), in Pa m$^5$ kg$^{-5/3}$ for $\mu_e=2$.
steps.hint: Choudhuri (5.10): $K_1=1.00\times10^7/\mu_e^{5/3}$ in SI, i.e. $\approx3.1\times10^6$ for $\mu_e=2$ (the constant evaluates to $3.12\times10^6$). It follows from $P=\frac{8\pi}{15h^3m_e}p_F^5$ with $p_F=(3h^3\rho/8\pi\mu_em_H)^{1/3}$.

steps.prompt: Pressure of the white-dwarf core, $P=K_1\rho^{5/3}$ with $\rho=10^9$ kg/m$^3$, in Pa.
steps.hint: $\approx3\times10^{21}$ Pa. Cross-check with $\frac25n_e\epsilon_F=\frac25\times3\times10^{35}\times160$ keV: same number. (Compare the Sun's centre, $\sim2.5\times10^{16}$ Pa.)

steps.prompt: How many times larger is $P_{\rm WD}$ than $P_{\rm Cu}$ (quick estimate within 25 %)?
steps.hint: $P\propto n^{5/3}$: $(3.5\times10^6)^{5/3}\approx8\times10^{10}$. Same physics, 11 decades of density.

encounters.title: How big is a white dwarf? Balance Pauli against gravity
encounters.problem: Estimate from energy balance (uniform sphere). $N$ electrons in a sphere of radius $R$ have kinetic energy $E_K=\frac35N\epsilon_F=A/R^2$ with $A=\frac35N\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\big(\frac{9\pi N}{4}\big)^{2/3}$ (since $n=3N/4\pi R^3$). Gravity gives $E_G=-B/R$ with $B=\frac35GM^2$ and $M=N\mu_em_H$. Equilibrium $dE/dR=0$ gives $R=2A/B$. White dwarf of $M=0.6\,M_\odot$, $\mu_e=2$. (Earth radius 6371 km.)

steps.hint: The Fermi kinetic energy scales as $1/R^2$ ($\epsilon_F\propto n^{2/3}\propto R^{-2}$): squeezing costs more and more.
Gravitational binding of a uniform sphere $\frac35GM^2/R$ scales as $1/R$ (weaker at small $R$ than the Pauli cost): that is why an equilibrium exists.
$R\approx8.5\times10^3$ km $\approx1.3$ Earth radii $\approx0.012R_\odot$: a white dwarf is Earth-sized with the mass of a star. Real $0.6M_\odot$ white dwarfs have $\approx8700$ km.
$\sim5\times10^8$ kg/m$^3$ $\approx5\times10^5$ g/cm$^3$: a teaspoon weighs a ton or more. The same order as the $10^9$ kg/m$^3$ assumed in the first quest (the core is denser than the mean).

steps.prompt: Mass–radius relation $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ (Choudhuri 5.25): radius of a $1.2\,M_\odot$ white dwarf in km.
steps.hint: Doubling the mass **shrinks** the star by $2^{-1/3}$: more massive white dwarfs are smaller. Minimising $A/R^2-B/R$ with $A\propto N^{5/3}$, $B\propto N^2$ gives $R\propto N^{-1/3}$.

encounters.title: The Chandrasekhar mass from the ultra-relativistic limit
encounters.problem: Now let the electrons be ultra-relativistic, $E=pc$: the mean energy per electron is $\frac34p_Fc$, so $E_K=\frac34\hbar c\,(9\pi/4)^{1/3}N^{4/3}/R=A'/R$. Both terms now scale as $1/R$, so there is a critical $N$ where $A'=B$ with $B=\frac35G(\mu_em_HN)^2$: for larger $N$ gravity wins at every radius and the star collapses. Setting $\frac34\hbar c(9\pi/4)^{1/3}N^{4/3}=\frac35G(\mu_em_HN)^2$ gives $N_{\rm Ch}^{2/3}=\dfrac{5}{4}\Big(\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\Big)^{1/3}\dfrac{\hbar c}{G\mu_e^2m_H^2}$. $\mu_e=2$.

steps.hint: $\hbar c/(Gm_H^2)=1.7\times10^{38}$ is the (squared) ratio of the electromagnetic-quantum to gravitational strength: $N_{\rm Ch}\sim(\hbar c/Gm_H^2)^{3/2}$. Only fundamental constants enter.
$\sim10^{57}$ electrons: $\sim2\times10^{57}$ nucleons, i.e. $\sim1.7\,M_\odot$.
$\approx1.7\,M_\odot$ from the uniform-sphere estimate, within 20 % of the exact value.

Evaluates to $1.43\,(2/\mu_e)^2M_\odot$ with these constants; Choudhuri quotes $1.46$ (5.28, rounded constants), the modern value is $1.44$. Neither mass depends on the star's radius: below it the star can sit anywhere on the $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ curve, at $M_{\rm Ch}$ it has $R\to0$ in this idealisation.

encounters.title: Photons and phonons: one derivation, two $T^3$ laws
encounters.problem: Cross-course (Solid State script 2.4, Astro photometry). A gas of bosons with $\omega=vq$ and $g$ polarisations has energy density $u=g\,\frac{\pi^2(k_BT)^4}{30(\hbar v)^3}$ and heat capacity per volume $c=4u/T$. Photons: $g=2$, $v=c$ (Planck). Phonons: $g=3$ with the mean sound speed $v$ (Debye). Use copper, $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ and $T_D=343$ K, where $\omega_D=v(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}$ defines $v$; and the CMB, $T=2.725$ K.

steps.hint: Photon gas: $g=2$, $v=c$ in the formula above. $a=7.566\times10^{-16}$ J m$^{-3}$K$^{-4}$; Stefan–Boltzmann $\sigma=ac/4$.

steps.prompt: Energy density of the cosmic microwave background $u=aT^4$ at $T=2.725$ K in J/m$^3$.
steps.hint: $4.2\times10^{-14}$ J/m$^3$ $=0.26$ eV/cm$^3$: the same CMB as in the astro room *Light Deck*.

steps.prompt: Mean sound velocity of copper from the Debye frequency, $v=k_BT_D/[\hbar(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}]$ in m/s.
steps.hint: $k_BT_D=\hbar\omega_D$ and $\omega_D=v\,q_D$ with $q_D=(6\pi^2n)^{1/3}$ the radius of the Debye sphere that holds $N$ states. $\approx2.6$ km/s (measured Cu: 3.8 km/s longitudinal, 2.3 km/s transverse).

steps.prompt: Phonon heat capacity per volume $c=4u/T=\frac{4}{T}\,3\frac{\pi^2(k_BT)^4}{30(\hbar v)^3}$ at $T=10$ K, in J m$^{-3}$K$^{-1}$.
steps.hint: Equals $\beta T^3$ with Debye's $\beta=\frac{12\pi^4}5nk_B/T_D^3=6.77$ J m$^{-3}$K$^{-4}$ (Phonon Halls): $6.8\times10^3$ J m$^{-3}$K$^{-1}$ at 10 K. The $6\pi^2n$ inside $\omega_D^3$ turns Debye's $\frac{12\pi^4}5$ into $\frac{2\pi^2}{5}$: the two derivations are the same.

steps.prompt: Photon heat capacity per volume at $T=10$ K, $c=4aT^3$, in J m$^{-3}$K$^{-1}$.
How many times larger is the phonon than the photon heat capacity at the same $T$ (quick estimate within a factor of 1.5)?
steps.hint: $\frac32(c/v)^3\approx2\times10^{15}$: low-energy excitations of matter are slow, and the cube of the velocity ratio is huge. Slow bosons mean many more states per energy.

encounters.title: Boss: Degenerate Matter (cross-course, constructed in exam style)

source.where: constructed from Solid State script 3.1 (Fermi gas), QM sheet 3 (box, counting of states) and Choudhuri §5.2-5.3 (pp. 129-137); no verbatim exam: the CLAUDE.md design calls for this cross-region boss

encounters.instructions: The same Fermi gas appears in three courses. Do it on paper, then enter the numbers.
statement: (a) [QM, 4 pt] A particle in a cubic box of side $L$ has states $\psi\propto\sin\frac{n_x\pi x}L\sin\frac{n_y\pi y}L\sin\frac{n_z\pi z}L$ with $E=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2mL^2}(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)$. Show that $N$ spin-$\frac12$ fermions fill all states up to $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$, $n=N/L^3$, and that $\epsilon_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}$ and $E_{\rm tot}=\frac35N\epsilon_F$.
(b) [Solid State, 4 pt] Evaluate $\epsilon_F$, $T_F$ and $P=\frac25n\epsilon_F$ for copper ($n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$). Why is $c_V\propto T$ and not $\frac32k_B$ per electron?

(c) [Astro, 6 pt] A white dwarf of mass $0.6M_\odot$ with $\mu_e=2$ is supported by non-relativistic electron degeneracy. Estimate its radius from $E=A/R^2-B/R$ and give the mean density. Which way does the radius change with mass?

(d) [Astro, 4 pt] For ultra-relativistic electrons both terms scale as $1/R$. Estimate the limiting mass $M_{\rm Ch}$ and comment on the exact value $\approx1.44\,(2/\mu_e)^2M_\odot$ (Choudhuri 5.28 quotes 1.46).
(e) [All, 2 pt] Why are electrons (not the nuclei) degenerate in a white dwarf, although the nuclei carry almost all the mass?
Game numbers: density of the core $\rho=10^{9}$ kg/m$^3$ for the Fermi energy; $M=0.6\,M_\odot$ for the radius.

finalAnswers.prompt: (b) Fermi temperature of copper in K.
(b) Degeneracy pressure of copper $\frac25n\epsilon_F$ in GPa.
(c) Fermi energy of the core ($\rho=10^9$ kg/m$^3$, $\mu_e=2$) in keV.
(c) Radius of the $0.6M_\odot$ white dwarf in km (energy balance).

keyPoints: (a) Each state is a point $(n_x,n_y,n_z)$ with $n_i>0$: one state per unit volume in $n$-space. The octant of a sphere of radius $n_F$ holds $\frac18\frac{4\pi}3n_F^3$ states, times 2 for spin: $N=\frac{\pi}3n_F^3$, $k_F=\pi n_F/L$, so $N=\frac{V}{3\pi^2}k_F^3$. $\epsilon_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m$; $E_{\rm tot}=\int^{\epsilon_F}\epsilon\,\nu(\epsilon)d\epsilon=\frac35N\epsilon_F$.

(b) $\epsilon_F=7.03$ eV, $T_F=8.2\times10^4$ K, $P=\frac25n\epsilon_F=38$ GPa. Only a fraction $T/T_F$ of the electrons (those within $k_BT$ of $\epsilon_F$, which have empty states available) can absorb heat: $c_V=\frac{\pi^2}3\nu(\epsilon_F)k_B^2T\propto T$.

(c) $N=M/\mu_em_H=3.6\times10^{56}$; $A=\frac35N\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}(9\pi N/4)^{2/3}$, $B=\frac35GM^2$; $dE/dR=0\Rightarrow R=2A/B\approx8.5\times10^3$ km (Earth-sized), $\bar\rho\sim5\times10^8$ kg/m$^3$. $R\propto M^{-1/3}$: heavier white dwarfs are smaller.

(d) Ultra-relativistic: $E_K=\frac34\hbar c(9\pi/4)^{1/3}N^{4/3}/R$ and gravity $-\frac35GM^2/R$: the two have the same $R$-dependence, so only the **mass** decides: for $N<N_{\rm Ch}$ the kinetic term wins and the star is stable, for $N>N_{\rm Ch}$ it collapses. $M_{\rm Ch}\approx1.7M_\odot$; solving Lane–Emden ($n=3$) gives $\approx1.43$-$1.46\,(2/\mu_e)^2M_\odot$ (Choudhuri 5.28).

(e) Equal kinetic energy $p^2/2m$ at the same $T$ gives light particles small momenta and thus a small phase-space volume; the electron number density in phase space is largest for electrons and reaches the Pauli limit $2/h^3$ first (Choudhuri §5.2). Nuclei remain non-degenerate and only supply the mass.

Connection to remember: the same $\frac35N\epsilon_F$ and $P=\frac25n\epsilon_F$ describe an electron in a metal, a neutron in a neutron star ($m\to m_n$) and electrons in a white dwarf. In QM it is a counting problem; in solids it explains $c_V\propto T$, $\chi_P$ and the bulk modulus; in astro it fixes $R(M)$ and $M_{\rm Ch}$.
